Figure 1: Comparison of different deepfake countermeasures. Although existing proactive forensic methods have achieved good performance, they are fundamentally constrained to single-face scenarios, neglecting multi-person scenarios which are closer to real-world applications. Our DAWF achieves not only source tracing but also the localization of forged faces in complex multi-person interaction scenes.
Figure 6: Localization precision comparisons of our DAWF and other competitive methods on the WIDERFace.

Figure 2: Analysis of detected face resolutions. Left: Histograms showing the frequency distribution of face image heights and widths. Right: Scatter plot displaying the joint distribution of face resolutions. The red “X” marker denotes the statistical centroid, centered near (62.4, 62.5).
Figure 8: Localization precision comparisons of our DAWF and other competitive methods on the CelebA-HQ.

Figure 3: Overall architecture of DAWF. (a) Training phase: The MFEncoder combines a face detector and a steganography kernel to output the encoded image Ien. After undergoing various distortions, the noised image Ino is passed to the MFTracer and MFLocalizer for watermark recovery and deepfake localization, respectively. (b) Testing phase: The MFTracer outputs the identity tracing information Mtr, and the MFLocalizer outputs the deepfake localization image Ilo. The ground-truth deepfake mask Imask generated by the noise layer is used to calculate the Intersection over Union (IoU) with the predicted forged face bounding boxes derived from Ilo. This facilitates a precise evaluation of the manipulated regions.
Figure 5: Localization results and visual quality under various typical distortions. Each column represents a distinct distortion type, with the localization results demonstrated by the red overlay.
